content: In children aged 12–17 years and weighing at least 35 kg, infected with hepatitis C virus (HCV) genotypes 2 or 3, a study conducted in April 2017 evaluated the pharmacokinetics (PK), safety, and efficacy of sofosbuvir (400 mg) combined with weight-based ribavirin (RBV). This open-label study included 52 adolescents, both treatment-naïve and treatment-experienced, across 28 sites in Australia, Germany, Italy, New Zealand, Russia, the United Kingdom, and the United States. The median age of participants was 15 years (range: 12–17 years), and the median body mass index (BMI) was 22 kg/m² (range: 16–32 kg/m²). The majority of participants were infected with HCV genotype 3a (71%), while smaller proportions were infected with genotypes 2 (12%), 2b (10%), 2a/2c (4%), and 4 (2%). Vertical transmission accounted for 73% of infections. Liver disease staging was unavailable for 60% of participants, while 42% had no cirrhosis. The study demonstrated a sustained virologic response at 12 weeks (SVR12) in 98% of the 52 adolescents treated. One patient with genotype 3 did not achieve SVR12 due to being lost to follow-up but did achieve SVR4. The most common adverse events were nausea (27%) and headache (23%). More than 10% of patients also experienced upper abdominal pain, diarrhea, asthenia, and dizziness. Seven patients (19%) experienced grade 3–4 adverse events, but none discontinued treatment due to these events. Mild, transient reductions in hemoglobin levels were observed, consistent with the known toxicity profile of ribavirin. All PK parameters were within predefined equivalence boundaries when compared to adults in phase 2 and phase 3 trials of the same medications. A similar trial is ongoing in children aged 3–12 years. In a separate registration trial (NCT 02249182), two adolescents with HCV genotype 3 were treated with sofosbuvir/ledipasvir (SOF/LED) for 12 weeks and achieved SVR12. However, the European Medicines Agency (EMA) has stated that Harvoni (SOF/LED) can be used for some patients with genotype 3, despite limited data in adolescents. Published trials in adults have shown high efficacy of SOF/LED and SOF/RBV regimens, with SVR rates exceeding 97%. The benefits of treating adolescents and children with HCV include the potential to eliminate viral hepatitis as a public health threat, particularly in high-burden countries. Highly effective direct-acting antiviral (DAA) regimens achieve cure rates exceeding 97%, and children may have even better SVR rates than adults. Early treatment can prevent liver-related complications, improve cognitive functioning, educational attainment, and overall well-being, and reduce the risk of horizontal transmission before the onset of high-risk behaviors. Additionally, treatment can alleviate the social stigma associated with HCV infection and reduce the long-term risk of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in adults who acquired HCV during childhood. Treating children is also cost-effective, as it avoids the higher costs associated with advanced liver disease in adulthood. For adolescents aged 12 years and older or weighing at least 35 kg, the recommended regimens include SOF/LED for 12 weeks for genotypes 1, 4, 5, or 6, and SOF with weight-based RBV for 12 weeks for genotype 2 and 24 weeks for genotype 3. Interferon (IFN)-based regimens should no longer be used due to their low efficacy, prolonged treatment duration, significant side effects (including growth deficits in children), and inconvenient administration via subcutaneous injections. For children under 12 years of age, treatment is deferred until they reach 12 years or until DAA regimens are approved for younger age groups. In exceptional cases, such as severe liver disease or high-risk conditions (e.g., HIV co-infection, thalassemia major, or childhood cancer survivors), IFN + RBV may be considered for genotypes 2 or 3. However, this approach is not ideal due to the suboptimal efficacy and safety profile of IFN-based regimens. The overall goal of treating HCV in childhood is to prevent liver damage, extrahepatic complications, and to achieve an HCV-free generation. The benefits of treatment outweigh the risks, especially as costs of DAAs continue to decrease globally. The inclusion of adolescents and children in treatment guidelines will encourage testing, case identification, and equitable access to curative therapies.
